templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener, passage-final clause
items.passage: Hummingbirds inhabiting the high Andes endure frigid nights by entering torpor, a hibernation-like state of drastically reduced metabolic activity. After falling more than 30 degrees below that of an active hummingbird during one such episode in 2020, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: a black metaltail’s torpor produced a body temperature of 3.26°C, the lowest yet reported for any bird.
a black metaltail registered a body temperature of 3.26°C, the lowest yet reported for any bird.
it was a black metaltail that registered a body temperature of 3.26°C, the lowest yet reported for any bird.
a black metaltail’s body temperature reached 3.26°C, the lowest yet reported for any bird.
items.explanation: The opening phrase says something fell below “that of an active hummingbird,” so the noun it describes must be the same kind of thing a hummingbird has, here a body temperature. Choice D places “a black metaltail’s body temperature” right after the phrase, so the sentence says the bird’s body temperature fell more than 30 degrees below the body temperature of an active hummingbird. In every other choice, “that” has nothing to stand for.

A.recipe: agent in possessive (P), wrong head noun
A.why_wrong: The head of “a black metaltail’s torpor” is “torpor,” a state, so the sentence illogically says the torpor fell below that (the torpor) of an active hummingbird.

B.why_wrong: “A black metaltail” follows the phrase, so the sentence says the bird itself fell below “that of an active hummingbird”; a bird cannot be compared with a hummingbird’s body temperature, so “that” has nothing to stand for.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the opening phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe.

sources.what: black metaltail (Metallura phoebe) minimum body temperature 3.26 °C, lowest yet reported for any bird; 26 birds of six species at about 3,800 m in the Andes, Wolf et al. 2020, Biology Letters
plain-language summary of the study

items.notes: Subject: natural science (zoology). Section 6: rule R3; key subject is a property of the obvious noun (the bird’s body temperature), forced by “that of” in the opener as in 2dd1b8bf and fced396a; three options open with “a black metaltail” so the head noun decides; options 14 to 19 words, key the shortest. Reviewer: opener rewritten from “After plummeting to 3.26°C”, which let B stand by metonymy (a bird “drops to” a temperature).
band7_moves: opener compares with “that of an active hummingbird”, so the right subject is a property built on the obvious noun (a black metaltail’s body temperature), as in 2dd1b8bf and fced396a
hardest distractor keeps every fact and starts with the obvious noun (a black metaltail registered), failing only because “that” has nothing to stand for, as fced396a A
a second possessive option with the wrong head (a black metaltail’s torpor), so the possessive form alone does not give the key away
options 14 to 19 words, equally grammatical as clauses; recipes W, P, E

fixes: second defensible option: with “After plummeting to 3.26°C”, B (a black metaltail set a record) stood by ordinary metonymy (a bird “drops to” a temperature); opener now “After falling more than 30 degrees below that of an active hummingbird”, so only a body temperature can fill “that of” (fced396a, 2dd1b8bf)
options rewritten to carry 3.26°C (A torpor, B the bird, C it-cleft, D body temperature); key letter unchanged
explanation, why_wrong, notes and band7_moves rewritten; re-solved blind after the fix: D only

band7.why: After the fix it is the 2dd1b8bf / fced396a pattern: “that of” in the opener makes the right subject a property of the obvious noun; B keeps every fact and starts with the obvious noun, failing only on what “that” can stand for; A is a second possessive with the wrong head; options 14 to 19 words.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener describing a component of the subject, passage-final clause
items.passage: The skin of at least 16 deep-sea fish species reflects less than 0.5 percent of incoming light, rendering the fishes nearly invisible amid bioluminescent flashes. Packed tightly into a continuous layer and considerably larger than those of ordinary black fishes, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: these fishes owe their darkness to pigment granules called melanosomes, which absorb nearly all incoming light.
the pigment granules called melanosomes in these fishes’ skin absorb nearly all incoming light.
these fishes’ skin absorbs nearly all incoming light by means of pigment granules called melanosomes.
it is pigment granules called melanosomes that allow these fishes’ skin to absorb nearly all incoming light.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes things that are packed into a layer and are larger than “those” (the same things) of ordinary black fishes. Only pigment granules fit that description, and choice B places “the pigment granules called melanosomes” right after the phrase. The fishes are not packed into a layer, and the singular “skin” cannot be compared with the plural “those.”

A.why_wrong: “These fishes” follows the phrase, so the sentence says the fishes are packed into a continuous layer and larger than those of ordinary black fishes.

C.recipe: agent in possessive (P), wrong head noun
C.why_wrong: The head of “these fishes’ skin” is “skin,” but the skin is not packed into a layer, and the plural “those” cannot refer back to the singular “skin.”

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the opening phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

sources.what: Davis, Thomas, Goetz, Robison, Johnsen, Osborn 2020, Current Biology: 16 species reflect less than 0.5% of light; melanosomes larger, more oblong and tightly packed into a continuous sheet
Pacific blackdragon among the ultra-black species

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine biology). Section 6: rule R3; key subject is a component of the obvious noun (the granules in these fishes’ skin); the opener’s plural “those” is the deciding clue against the singular “skin”; options 14 to 18 words, key not the longest. Blind solve: only B names plural things that can be packed into a layer.
band7_moves: opener built on a comparison with “those of”, so the right subject is a part of the obvious noun, as “that of” works in 2dd1b8bf and fced396a
two distractors start with the obvious noun or its possessive (these fishes, these fishes’ skin), the second ruled out only by the number of “those”
key does not echo the passage: melanosomes are named only in the options
options 14 to 18 words; recipes W, P, E

band7.why: Same pattern: “those of ordinary black fishes” binds the subject to a component of the obvious noun (the granules); A starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact; C, the possessive “these fishes’ skin”, fails only on the number of “those”; melanosomes appear only in the options.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final clause
items.passage: In a 2018 laboratory study, ecologists Shinji Sugiura and Takuya Sato fed bombardier beetles to Japanese toads, which swallowed every beetle offered. Spraying hot chemicals inside the toads’ stomachs, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: nearly half of the toads vomited the beetles back up, alive and active, within two hours.
the beetles’ spray made nearly half of the toads vomit them back up within two hours.
the beetles caused nearly half of the toads to vomit them back up within two hours.
the vomiting of the beetles by nearly half of the toads occurred within two hours.
items.explanation: The beetles are the ones spraying hot chemicals inside the toads’ stomachs. Choice C places “the beetles” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes them.

A.why_wrong: “Nearly half of the toads” follows the phrase, so the sentence says the toads sprayed chemicals inside their own stomachs.

B.why_wrong: The head of “the beetles’ spray” is “spray,” so the sentence illogically says the spray was spraying hot chemicals.

D.why_wrong: “The vomiting of the beetles” follows the phrase, so the sentence says the vomiting sprayed hot chemicals.

sources.what: Sugiura and Sato 2018, Biology Letters: all toads (Bufo japonicus, B. torrenticola) swallowed the beetles; 43% vomited them 12 to 107 minutes later, all alive; beetles eject hot chemicals inside the toads
study data record

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ecology). Band 6: plain agent as the right subject, three distractor recipes (W, P, N). Blind solve: only C makes the sprayers the subject.

band7.why: band_target 6; plain agent subject (the beetles) as in 3.5 and 3.14; the opener’s “the toads’ stomachs” makes the toad-subject option tempting; recipes W, P, N.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: The scaly-foot snail inhabits hydrothermal vents in the Indian Ocean. A three-layered structure mineralized with iron sulfide, ______ dissipates much of the energy of a crab’s pinch, confining fractures to tiny regions surrounding the point of contact, computer simulations suggest.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the scaly-foot snail, thanks to its shell,
it is the scaly-foot snail’s shell that
the shell’s outer layer of iron sulfide
items.explanation: The opening phrase “A three-layered structure mineralized with iron sulfide” describes the snail’s shell. Choice A makes “the scaly-foot snail’s shell” the subject right after the phrase, so the phrase and the noun it describes sit together.

B.why_wrong: “The scaly-foot snail” follows the phrase, so the sentence says the snail itself is a three-layered structure mineralized with iron sulfide.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase describes nothing logical.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W), part of the right noun
D.why_wrong: “The shell’s outer layer” is a single layer, not a three-layered structure, so the opening phrase cannot describe it.

sources.what: three-layered shell: iron sulfide outer layer, thick organic middle layer, calcified inner layer; simulated crab-claw penetration; cracks localized as microcracks around the impact (Yao, Ortiz et al. 2010, PNAS)
same study, energy absorption by the organic middle layer

items.notes: Subject: natural science (biology, materials). No band-7 official item exists for R3_appositive (band-6 models 3.7, 3.12, 2b6e1c06); band-7 settings applied from section 5. Section 6: rule R3; 21 run words follow the blank; key subject is a possessive built on the obvious noun; options 4 to 7 words, key the shortest. Blind solve: only A names the structure the opener describes.
band7_moves: key subject is a part named through the obvious noun (the scaly-foot snail’s shell), as Iceland’s parliament in 2b6e1c06
hardest distractor keeps the obvious noun as subject and every fact (the scaly-foot snail, thanks to its shell)
a second distractor starts with a part of the right noun (the shell’s outer layer), one level too deep
mid-sentence blank with 21 run words after it, so each option must also fit the downstream verb dissipates

fixes: D why_wrong: dropped the claim that an iron sulfide layer cannot be mineralized with iron sulfide (not a sound reason)
band_target left at 7 (as the transitions reviewer did); verdict strong band 6, the template has no band-7 official

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md section 5 and appendix), so it cannot be band 7. Strong band 6 on 2b6e1c06: key a possessive built on the obvious noun, D one level too deep (a single layer is not a three-layered structure), mid-sentence blank with 21 run words after it.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head with a plural of-phrase and a dash interrupter
items.passage: Mexican designer Fernando Laposse produces Totomoxtle, a decorative veneer for furniture and interiors, from the husks of heirloom maize cultivated by Mixtec farmers in Tonahuixtla, Puebla. The astonishing range of colors in these husks—shades from deep purple to pale cream—______ attributable to indigenous varieties that the farmers revived using seeds preserved for decades in a seed bank.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “range”; “of colors in the husks” and the dash interrupter only describe it. The singular verb “is” agrees with “range.”

A.why_wrong: The plural “are” agrees with “colors,” “husks” or “shades,” not with the singular subject “range.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “were” does not agree with the singular subject “range.”

D.why_wrong: The plural “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “range.”

sources.what: Totomoxtle: husks of native corn ironed flat and glued to a backing; colors from deep purple to soft cream; Mixtec farmers of Tonahuixtla, Puebla
seeds from a seed bank’s vaults used to reintroduce near-extinct varieties

items.notes: Subject: arts (design). Band 6: three plural attractors (colors, husks, shades) between the singular head and the blank. Blind solve: only is agrees with range.

band7.why: band_target 6; singular head with three plural attractors (colors, husks, shades) and a dash interrupter, 17 run words after the blank, as 3.2 and c91ef0f0.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: plain plural plus generic plural possessor
items.passage: To human ears, a squabbling Egyptian fruit bat’s calls all sound alike. Yet analyzing nearly 15,000 such calls, a machine-learning algorithm could often identify the ______ disputes: food, perches, sleeping positions, or mating.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first noun names several things (the list after the colon gives four), so it takes the plain plural “subjects.” The disputes are those of fruit bats in general, so the second noun takes the plural possessive “bats’.” With no article before it, a singular possessive such as “bat’s” cannot stand.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Subject’s” is a singular possessive, but the context needs the plain plural “subjects”; nothing belongs to a subject here.

C.why_wrong: “Bat’s” is singular, and a singular noun here would need an article (“a bat’s” or “the bat’s”); the disputes are those of bats in general, so the plural possessive “bats’” is needed.

D.why_wrong: “Bats” is a plain plural, but the disputes belong to the bats, so the possessive “bats’” is needed.

sources.what: Prat, Taub, Yovel 2016, Scientific Reports: 14,863 calls of seven adult females analysed; contexts feeding, perch, sleep and mating aggression; context classified at 61% vs 25% chance

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal communication). Section 6: rule R6; two slots, the second a generic plural possessor with no article (bats’ disputes), as objects’ movement in 2784cbaf. Reviewer: hardened from “the bats’” after “seven captive Egyptian fruit bats”, where the plural cue sat in the same sentence.
band7_moves: two slots, the second a generic plural possessor with no article (bats’ disputes), as objects’ movement in 2784cbaf

the setup uses the singular possessive (a squabbling Egyptian fruit bat’s calls), which pulls toward bat’s as “an object” does in the model; bat’s fails by construction, since a singular count noun needs an article
needless apostrophe on the plain plural (subject’s), the one-slot error students miss when they focus on the second noun
frame changed from the model: of-phrase and colon list instead of a relative clause

fixes: hardened (read band 6: the plural cue “seven captive Egyptian fruit bats” sat 7 words before “the bats’”): setup now a squabbling Egyptian fruit bat’s calls, possessor now the generic plural with no article (subjects of bats’), as 2784cbaf; bat’s fails by construction
explanation, why_wrong, notes and band7_moves rewritten; re-solved blind after the fix: B only

band7.why: After the fix it mirrors 2784cbaf: two slots, a generic plural possessor with no article, and a singular possessive in the setup (a squabbling Egyptian fruit bat’s calls) pulling toward bat’s, as “an object” does in the model.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose infinitive after a three-verb compound predicate
items.passage: Cognitive scientists Can Kabadayi and Mathias Osvath trained five ravens to operate a puzzle apparatus by inserting a stone, removed the apparatus, and presented the stone alongside unsuitable objects ______ whether the birds would select it and retain it until the apparatus reappeared 15 minutes later.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence already has its three finite verbs, “trained,” “removed,” and “presented,” joined by “and.” The blank must begin a phrase explaining why the researchers presented the objects, and the to-infinitive “to test” does that.

B.recipe: wrong nonfinite (participle instead of purpose infinitive)
B.why_wrong: Without a comma, “testing” attaches to the nearest noun, so the sentence illogically says the unsuitable objects were testing whether the birds would choose the stone.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: “Tested” would be a fourth finite verb added to a series that is already closed by “and presented,” and there is no conjunction to join it.

D.why_wrong: “And testing” is not parallel with the past tense verbs “trained,” “removed,” and “presented,” and as a participle it has no main clause to attach to.

sources.what: Kabadayi and Osvath 2017, Science: five ravens taught to use a stone on a puzzle box; box absent the next day; birds chose the stone over decoys; box returned 15 minutes later

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal cognition). No band-7 official item exists for R2_to_inf (band-6 model 3.19); band-7 settings applied from section 5. Section 6: run 46 words, 15 run words after the blank; options vary on finiteness and attachment. Blind solve: only to test fits a sentence whose verb series is already closed.
band7_moves: three-verb compound predicate closed by and before the blank, so a fourth finite verb (tested) reads as a natural next step until the closed series is noticed
the noun right before the blank (unsuitable objects) makes the bare participle illogical, the trap CB names for 3.19
run of 46 words with 15 words after the blank
options kept to the 3.19 set (to V, V-ing, V-ed, and V-ing) so the student must reject two nonfinite forms as well as the finite one

fixes: band_target left at 7 (as the transitions reviewer did); verdict strong band 6, the template has no band-7 official

band7.why: R2_to_inf has no band-7 official items (section 5 and appendix), so it cannot be band 7. Strong band 6 on 3.19: verb series closed by “and presented”, 46-word run with 15 words after the blank, bare “testing” attaches to “unsuitable objects” (CB’s own 3.19 rationale).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head with a plural noun in the of-phrase
items.passage: The nonprofit GiveDirectly has distributed unconditional cash transfers to impoverished households in western Kenya. A 2016 evaluation of the transfers ______ that recipients of a single lump sum were more likely than monthly recipients to purchase durable assets such as metal roofs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “evaluation”; the phrase “of the transfers” only describes it. The singular verb “suggests” agrees with “evaluation.”

A.why_wrong: The plural “suggest” agrees with “transfers,” the noun right before the blank, not with the singular subject “evaluation.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “are suggesting” does not agree with the singular subject “evaluation.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “have suggested” does not agree with the singular subject “evaluation.”

sources.what: Haushofer and Shapiro 2016, QJE: GiveDirectly transfers in Rarieda, western Kenya; lump-sum recipients more likely to invest in assets such as metal roofs

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Medium: the plural attractor transfers sits right before the blank. Blind solve: only suggests is singular.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural antecedent with a singular rival noun before the blank
items.passage: In a 2014 experiment, Hadza hunter-gatherers in northern Tanzania each received an inexpensive item, such as a lighter, and were then offered a comparable item in exchange. Participants from isolated camps traded roughly half the time, but those residing near a commercial village typically kept whatever ______ had received.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “those residing near a commercial village,” a plural group of Hadza. The plural pronoun “they” agrees with that antecedent.

A.why_wrong: The singular “it” matches the nearby “village” or “item,” but the people who had received the items are the plural “those.”

B.why_wrong: “One” is singular and generic, so it does not agree with the plural “those” and blurs who received the item.

D.why_wrong: “We” is first person, but the Hadza are referred to in the third person.

sources.what: Apicella, Azevedo, Christakis, Fowler 2014, AER: isolated Hadza showed no endowment effect, market-exposed Hadza did; items were biscuits and lighters; isolated group traded about half the time

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics, anthropology). Medium: singular rival nouns (village, item) sit between the antecedent and the blank. Blind solve: only they agrees with those.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + plural noun, options carry the comma
items.passage: Formerly enslaved quilter Harriet Powers exhibited her Bible Quilt at an 1886 cotton fair in Georgia. Artist Jennie Smith offered to purchase it, but Powers sold it only years later, for five dollars. Smith transcribed Powers’s commentary on the ______ which illustrate biblical episodes such as Jacob’s dream and the Crucifixion.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The panels belong to one quilt, the Bible Quilt, so the singular possessive “quilt’s” is needed. There are eleven panels, and nothing belongs to them, so the plain plural “panels” is needed.

B.why_wrong: “Quilts” is a plain plural, but the panels belong to the quilt, so a possessive is needed.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Panel’s” is a singular possessive, but the context needs the plain plural “panels.”

D.why_wrong: “Quilts’” is a plural possessive, but the panels belong to a single quilt.

sources.what: Bible Quilt shown at the 1886 Athens cotton fair; Jennie Smith, artist and art teacher, bought it years later for five dollars and recorded Powers’s explanations; 11 panels including Jacob’s dream and the Crucifixion

items.notes: Subject: arts and history. Medium: two-slot grid as in 2.14 and 2.24; number cues her Bible Quilt and eleven. Blind solve: quilt’s + panels.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: compound subject (two titles joined by and) with a singular each-phrase between
items.passage: Higuchi Ichiyō’s “Takekurabe” (“Child’s Play”) and “Nigorie” (“Troubled Waters”), each portraying a young heroine whose future is constrained by poverty in Meiji-era Tokyo, ______ published in 1895, a year before the writer died of tuberculosis at age 24.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is compound: two stories, “Takekurabe” and “Nigorie,” joined by “and”; the phrase beginning with “each” only describes them. The plural verb “were” agrees with the compound subject.

A.why_wrong: The singular “was” agrees with “each” or “a young heroine,” and echoes the singular “is” inside the phrase, but the compound subject names two stories.

C.why_wrong: The singular “is” does not agree with the compound subject.

D.why_wrong: The singular “has been” does not agree with the compound subject.

sources.what: Takekurabe and Nigorie both 1895; died 23 November 1896 at 24 of tuberculosis
plots: a 14-year-old girl near Yoshiwara; Oriki, a sake-shop waitress

items.notes: Subject: literature. Medium: compound subject followed by an each-phrase with singular nouns and a singular verb (is constrained), as 2.13. Blind solve: only were is plural.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener naming a person, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: A respected medicine woman from the Tongva village of Jachivit, ______ leaders of neighboring villages to join a 1785 uprising against Mission San Gabriel, where Franciscan missionaries had prohibited ceremonial dancing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Spanish authorities accused Toypurina of rallying
it was Toypurina who agreed to rally
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a medicine woman, Toypurina. Choice D places “Toypurina” right after the phrase, so the phrase describes the right person.

A.why_wrong: “Spanish authorities” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says a group of authorities was a respected medicine woman from Jachivit.

B.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, which leaves the phrase describing nothing logical.

C.why_wrong: The head of “Toypurina’s influence” is “influence,” so the sentence says the influence was a medicine woman.

sources.what: Toypurina, Tongva medicine woman of Jachivit, recruited by Nicolás José after the ban on dances; contacted other village leaders; 1785 attack on Mission San Gabriel

items.notes: Subject: history. Medium: short appositive opener and a person as the right subject, as 2.10. Blind solve: only D puts the medicine woman first.

fixes: A was “Nicolás José recruited Toypurina to rally”, killed only by knowing Nicolás is a man’s name; now “Spanish authorities accused Toypurina of rallying” (plural group, cannot be a medicine woman)

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural object pronoun after of
items.passage: Vietnamese Danish artist Danh Võ’s We the People (2011–2016) is a full-scale replica of the Statue of Liberty’s copper exterior, fabricated in Shanghai as approximately 250 separate components. Võ has never assembled the components, instead displaying dozens of ______ at a time in more than 15 countries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “the components,” a plural noun. The plural pronoun “them” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The singular “it” does not agree with the plural antecedent “the components,” and “dozens of it” is not idiomatic.

C.why_wrong: The singular “this” does not agree with the plural “the components.”

D.why_wrong: The singular “that” does not agree with the plural “the components.”

sources.what: We the People: 1:1 copper replica of the Statue of Liberty in about 250 pieces, fabricated in Shanghai, never assembled; 2014 New York display of fifty sections
dates 2011 to 2016; shown in more than fifteen countries

items.notes: Subject: arts. Easy: antecedent is the object of the same sentence’s first clause. Blind solve: dozens of them.

fixes: originality confirmed: official 9d4f331c (Transitions) is about Bartholdi and Eiffel designing the statue’s arm; this item is about Võ’s unassembled replica, no shared wording

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: singular subject pronoun
items.passage: Since the 1860s, lichens have been characterized as symbiotic partnerships between a fungus and an alga. In 2016, however, lichenologist Toby Spribille identified a third participant in numerous lichens: a basidiomycete yeast. ______ inhabits the cortex, the lichen’s protective outer layer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “a basidiomycete yeast,” a singular noun, and its verb “inhabits” is singular. The singular pronoun “It” agrees with the antecedent.

A.why_wrong: The plural “They” does not agree with the singular “yeast” or with the verb “inhabits.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “Those” does not agree with the singular “yeast.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “Some” does not agree with the singular “yeast.”

sources.what: Spribille et al. 2016, Science: basidiomycete yeasts in the cortex of macrolichens, a probable third partner

items.notes: Subject: natural science (biology). Easy, as 1.39. Blind solve: It.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular name with a singular appositive
items.passage: Nana Asmaʼu, daughter of Usman dan Fodio, founder of the Sokoto Caliphate in present-day Nigeria, ______ an accomplished poet, scholar, and educator who composed religious, historical, and instructional verse in three languages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “Nana Asmaʼu,” one person; the appositive between the commas only describes her. The singular verb “was” agrees with the subject.

B.why_wrong: The plural “are” does not agree with the singular subject “Nana Asmaʼu.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “have been” does not agree with the singular subject.

D.why_wrong: The plural “were” does not agree with the singular subject.

sources.what: Nana Asma’u (1793 to 1864), daughter of Usman dan Fodio; poet and teacher writing in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa

items.notes: Subject: literature and history. Easy: singular appositive, no number clash, as 1.4. Blind solve: was.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head with a plural of-phrase
items.passage: Males of several deep-sea anglerfish species ______ permanently fused to considerably larger females, a reproductive strategy that a 2020 genetic analysis linked to the loss of crucial immune genes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the plural noun “Males.” The plural verb “are” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: The singular “is” does not agree with the plural subject “Males.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “was” does not agree with the plural subject.

D.why_wrong: The singular “has been” does not agree with the plural subject.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for habitual behavior, parallel with present verbs
items.passage: At a site in Australia’s Jervis Bay known as Octlantis, as many as 15 gloomy octopuses—animals generally considered solitary—live in close proximity. The octopuses ______ in dens dug into accumulated mounds of discarded scallop shells and frequently signal to, pursue, or even evict their neighbors.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes what the octopuses habitually do, and the blank is the first verb of a compound predicate whose other verbs, “signal,” “pursue,” and “evict,” are simple present. The simple present “shelter” keeps the verbs parallel and fits octopuses that live there now.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “sheltered” is not parallel with “signal,” “pursue,” and “evict,” and it suggests the octopuses no longer shelter there, though the passage says they live there now.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had sheltered” places the action before another past event, but the passage describes ongoing behavior.

C.why_wrong: The past progressive “were sheltering” is not parallel with the present tense verbs that share its subject.

A.why_wrong: “Artists” lacks the possessive apostrophe, and “sculpture’s” is a possessive where a plain plural is needed.

B.why_wrong: “Sculpture’s” is a singular possessive, but the context needs the plain plural “sculptures.”

D.why_wrong: “Artists” is a plain plural, but the sculptures belong to the artist, so “artist’s” is needed.
